A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CauKer and retain corresponding methods, experiments and appendices. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the equations, tables and figures, including the expanded v3 appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original UCR classification experiments, data/model/training-time scaling results, and analyses of synthetic data and learned representations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds runtime, sensitivity, WOODS, forecasting, fine-tuning and irregular clinical-data experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the stated causal propagation rule: v1 applies edge activations before linear aggregation, whereas v3 applies an activation after aggregating parents. The GP construction, function banks and pretraining losses remain unchanged. Edge-based descriptions elsewhere remain inconsistent, so the implemented behavior is not fully resolved.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained UCR evaluation and pretraining corpora, v3 evaluates 17 WOODS datasets, irregular multivariate clinical classification on P12/P19, and forecasting on 27 chronos-zero-shot subsets. These substantially extend the represented domains, input conditions and prediction tasks.

E2.justification: The original SCM, FPFN, KernelSynth and Mean-KernelSynth comparison is retained. v3 adds raw-series Logistic Regression, XGBoost and Random Forest comparisons, the supervised WOODS ERM baseline, and official Chronos checkpoints plus Seasonal Naive in forecasting. These are reported comparisons, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: The original frozen-encoder UCR protocol and training budgets are retained. New protocols include supervised downstream fine-tuning, clinical evaluation with AUROC/AUPRC, Chronos forecasting with MASE, controlled generation timing for 1,000 length-512 series, and distribution alignment using 512 random projections. These substantially expand evaluation procedures rather than establish reruns of existing experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds kernel/parent and DAG-size sensitivity sweeps, single-kernel failure tests, SWD/CKNNA alignment analysis, domain-wise UCR results, PCA coverage plots, and ECG/Fish attention-rollout case studies. The earlier DTW clustering, nonlinearity/CKA and UMAP analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly reports means and standard deviations across five independent synthetic draws. Section 4.4 adds a two-sided Wilcoxon forecasting comparison with p=0.84 at significance level 0.05. These are localized additions; repeated-training uncertainty is still not reported for the headline UCR accuracies.

E6.justification: The original generator comparison and data/model scaling tables retain their values. Numerous results are newly reported: Table 10 gives WOODS averages of 0.820 for CauKer100K, 0.810 for original Mantis and 0.800 for ERM; Table 12 gives fine-tuning accuracies of 0.8291/0.8457 for CauKer100K/1M versus 0.8496 for original Mantis. Table 13 shows CauKer1M outperforming the baseline on P12 but trailing on P19. Runtime, sensitivity, alignment and forecasting results are also added.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the formal activation map from edges to vertices and reverses the order of nonlinear activation and linear aggregation. This is a local, mathematically non-equivalent specification change. Neither version develops new theorems or proofs; the added standard metric formulas mainly document evaluation.

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory findings and conclusion retain the same central contributions: classification-oriented GP/SCM generation, sample-efficient synthetic-only pretraining, and clearer scaling behavior than with the studied real datasets. The added applications support these claims without redefining them. Removing 'only' from the title does not remove the synthetic-only claim from the paper.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of kernel diversity and failure modes, embedding coverage, domain-specific gains and deficits, attention localization, and transfer to forecasting and supervised adaptation. It also discusses possible multivariate applicability while specifying univariate pretraining. v1's separate comparison with forecasting scaling laws, including its sub-exponential-growth qualification, is removed. The original in-distribution caveat for official checkpoints is retained and emphasized.

D1.justification: v1's pseudocode subsection contains only prose; v3 supplies Algorithm 1 with sampling, graph traversal and output construction details. v3 also adds a CauKer source-code link and documents procedures for the new forecasting, alignment and visualization experiments. These substantially improve documented reproducibility, although some implementation choices remain ambiguous and repository availability was not externally verified.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to newer TSFMs, vision-based approaches, synthetic-data research, and the new benchmarks and analysis tools. Edwards et al. (2025) and Shi et al. (2024) disappear with the forecasting-scaling discussion. The added positioning paragraph largely reinforces the existing distinction from forecasting generators and tabular SCMs rather than changing the novelty claim.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable. v3 locally rewrites protocol and motivation passages, removes the forecasting-scaling subsection, adds an appendix roadmap and disclosures, and updates the title, authors and affiliations. The additional scientific sections do not amount to a wholesale rewrite of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adds the algorithm display, numerous experimental tables, PCA figures and attention-rollout panels. Figure 3's staggered plot groups become a single row, and existing kernel, mean-function and embedding illustrations are resized or relocated. The document template, headings and figure placement also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's UCR-centered evidence through WOODS, irregular clinical, forecasting and fine-tuning evaluations, including mixed outcomes that expose applicability limits. Sensitivity and failure analyses address previously untested generator choices, while Algorithm 1 and code-access information address documentation gaps. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses, including unresolved activation descriptions, limited training uncertainty reporting, and the WOODS discrepancy of 11 wins in Table 10 versus 12 in the prose.
